narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 53.1% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. This lower standing signaled to the model a higher risk that you might struggle with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.30 it sits slightly above the 3.23 average of accepted students, giving the model some reassurance that you have the baseline ability to succeed. Similarly, your LSAT score of 35 was a modest negative influence; while close to the 37.18 average of accepted applicants, it still pulled the prediction slightly toward passing rather than failing.

Taken together, the model concluded that your third-year class rank created more risk than your solid grades and test score could offset. 

What you should do next is straightforward: strengthen the areas the model weighed most heavily. Focus on raising your academic performance in the remaining years so your class rank improves, consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise it meaningfully, and then reapply. Many students in similar situations have successfully turned their applications around by targeting exactly these academic signals.
